## Overview

Functions that aid in exploration of models from the packages MCMCglmm and lme4.

## Installation

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Install this development version from GitHub:
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("Euphrasiologist/VCVglmm")
```

## Dependencies

Please install them as follows:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("MCMCglmm"); install.packages("lme4")
library(MCMCglmm); library(lme4)

install.packages("data.table"); install.packages("tidyverse"); install.packages("ape"); install.packages("coda"); install.packages("lattice")
library(data.table); library(ggplot2); library(plyr); library(dplyr); library(reshape2); library(ape); library("coda"); library("lattice")
```

## Simulation data and examples of how the functions can be used

Our toy data set will contain six parasites and six hosts, with 15 replicates of each parasite on each host. The response variable, Pterm, is simulated through normal deviations, with each parasite having different means, regardless of host (as we shall see...).

```{r, echo=FALSE}
library(data.table)
dat.1 <- data.frame(
  
  "Parasite" = rep(paste("P", 1:6, sep = ""), 90),
  "Hosts" = rep(paste("H", 1:6, sep = ""), 90)
  
)

# order the Hosts vector
dat.1$Hosts <- dat.1$Hosts[order(dat.1$Hosts)]
# create a blank vector to be filled
dat.1$Pterm <- vector(length = 540)

## Each Euphrasia has values sampled from a poisson distribution of different means
dat.1$Pterm[dat.1$Parasite == "P1"] <- rnorm(n = 90, mean = 5, sd = 2)
dat.1$Pterm[dat.1$Parasite == "P2"] <- rnorm(n = 90, mean = 10, sd = 2)
dat.1$Pterm[dat.1$Parasite == "P3"] <- rnorm(n = 90, mean = 15, sd = 2)
dat.1$Pterm[dat.1$Parasite == "P4"] <- rnorm(n = 90, mean = 20, sd = 2)
dat.1$Pterm[dat.1$Parasite == "P5"] <- rnorm(n = 90, mean = 25, sd = 2)
dat.1$Pterm[dat.1$Parasite == "P6"] <- rnorm(n = 90, mean = 30, sd = 2)

setDT(dat.1)

```

We can fit models to a very simple dataset about growth of parasites on host species.

```{r, eval=TRUE}
head(dat.1); tail(dat.1)
```

Firstly we will do a model in lme4. 

```{r}
library(lme4)

mod.1 <- lmer(Pterm ~ 1 + (1 | Hosts) + (1 | Parasite), data = dat.1)

summary(mod.1)
```

So this shows that almost all of the variance in our Pterm is being explained by Parasite, and the rest by the residual. But let's check that further...

```{r}
library(VCVglmm)
VarExpl.mer(mod.1)
```

And if we want that pesky p-value that lme4 doesn't give you in the `summary()`, don't worry.

```{r}
calc_pvals(mod.1)
```

And if we quickly translate that to `MCMCglmm()` language...

```{r}
library(MCMCglmm)

mod.2 <- MCMCglmm(Pterm ~ 1, 
                  random = ~ Hosts + Parasite,
                  data = dat.1,
                  pr = TRUE,
                  verbose = FALSE)

summary(mod.2)
```

Looks sensible to me, we might want to add a prior for real data however. Below, using `Solapply()` we can extract the posterior modes of each of the levels of the random effects to see which levels are having the greatest impact.

```{r}
Solapply(mod.2)
```

Again we see that ~95%+ of the variability in our data is explained by Parasite, which was pretty much 100% in the lmer model.

```{r}
MCMCRepnorm2(mod = mod.2)
```

## Diagnosing and explaining models

### A plain-English summary

`glmm_explain()` works on `MCMCglmm`, `lmer` and `glmer` models. It reports:

- convergence and fit checks;
- each fixed effect on the latent (link) scale and on the data scale. Rate ratios and changes in expected counts for Poisson models, odds ratios and changes in probability for binary models, all averaged over the random effects;
- the variance explained by each random term on the latent, link and data scales;
- marginal and conditional R².

```{r, eval = FALSE}
glmm_explain(mod.2)
```

### Variance partitioning and R²

`glmm_varpart()` generalises `MCMCRepnorm2()` and `MCMCReppois()` to Gaussian, Poisson, binary (logit/probit), ordinal and threshold models. It also handles random slopes and `idh()`/`us()` structures, with each term's variance averaged over the observations. Proportions are given on three scales:

- latent;
- link, which adds the distribution-specific variance;
- data, the observed scale, computed exactly or by Gauss-Hermite quadrature.

`glmm_R2()` gives Nakagawa & Schielzeth's marginal and conditional R².

These work on multi-response models (`cbind(y1, y2) ~ trait - 1 + ...`), giving results per trait with that trait's family. Ordinal and threshold models with more than two categories are also supported: their data scale uses the cutpoints and refers to the category number. Categorical responses with more than two categories get the latent scale per log-odds contrast, and the data scale per category: the variance in each category indicator explained by each term, computed jointly over the contrasts by simulation. `glmm_explain()` also reports how each covariate changes every category's probability. `glmm_cor()` extracts every correlation in the covariance structures, for example among-group vs residual correlations between traits, or intercept-slope correlations.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
vp <- glmm_varpart(mod.2, fixed = TRUE)
vp
plot(vp)
glmm_R2(mod.2)
glmm_cor(mv.mod)   # correlations, e.g. for a multi-response model
```

### MCMC diagnostics

```{r, eval = FALSE}
MCMCdiag(mod.2)                 # ESS, autocorrelation, Geweke, Heidelberger-Welch, boundary variances, correlated fixed effects...
MCMCtrace(mod.2)                # ggplot2 traces with running means; pass a list of models to overlay chains
MCMCacfplot(mod.2)              # autocorrelation by lag
MCMCcorplot(mod.2)              # posterior correlations between fixed effects
MCMCpriorplot(mod.2, prior)     # is the posterior any different from the prior?
MCMCgelman(chain1, chain2, chain3)  # Gelman-Rubin R-hat across chains
```

### lme4 diagnostics

```{r, eval = FALSE}
merdiag(mod.1)      # convergence, singular fits, few levels, overdispersion, collinearity, separation
merdiagplot(mod.1)  # residuals vs fitted, QQ plots of residuals and random effects, scale-location
```
